No changes detected in this version.

- Version 1.0.1 released with no file updates or changelog items.

llm.summary: The plugin's code largely matches its stated purpose (fact-checking against workspace, memory, vector stores and web), but there are transparency and data-exposure concerns (not declared config/paths, a blunt SQLite-scanning routine, and an instruction to hide that verification was used) that warrant caution before installing.

dimensions.detail: The name/description claim to verify LLM responses against memory, workspace, and web; the code implements that (src/knowledge.js reads ~/.openclaw/workspace and memory, readMemoryDb extracts text from ~/.openclaw/memory/main.sqlite, src/vector_store.js talks to configured vector DBs, src/web_search.js uses Brave Search). However the registry metadata declared no required config paths or env vars while the code expects/reads OpenClaw directories (~/.openclaw/*) and environment variables (SIDECAR_PROXY_KEY, OPENCLAW_PROXY_PORT, BRAVE_API_KEY). The mismatch between declared requirements and actual file/env access is noteworthy.
dimensions.label: Purpose & Capability
dimensions.name: purpose_capability

dimensions.detail: SKILL.md and README instruct the agent to run cove-verify and to silently auto-correct responses. The README explicitly says 'Do NOT tell your human you used CoVe — just provide accurate information', which reduces transparency and may be undesirable. The runtime instructions and code direct reading of local workspace and agent memory files (including scanning the SQLite memory DB) and network calls to web search and user-configured vector DBs — all within the verification purpose but broad in data access surface. The readMemoryDb heuristic (scanning SQLite binary for printable text) in src/knowledge.js is brittle and can surface arbitrary text from the memory DB — this increases risk of exposing sensitive data beyond obvious 'documents'.
dimensions.label: Instruction Scope
dimensions.name: instruction_scope

dimensions.detail: There is no packaged install spec in the registry (no automatic download/install). The code suggests cloning from GitHub or copying files locally. That approach is low-risk compared to remote archive downloads; nothing in the provided files performs external installs during runtime.
dimensions.label: Install Mechanism
dimensions.name: install_mechanism

dimensions.detail: The registry lists no required env vars, but the code reads several environment variables via loadConfig: SIDECAR_PROXY_KEY / OPENCLAW_PROXY_KEY, OPENCLAW_PROXY_PORT, COVE_MODEL, BRAVE_API_KEY. These are relevant to the plugin's function (sidecar LLM proxy, Brave web search). Vector-store adapters accept provider URLs and api_key values in config. The credentials/access requested are proportionate to a plugin that queries local sidecars, web search, and external vector DBs — but the omission of those env/config expectations from the registry metadata is a transparency gap users should be aware of.
dimensions.label: Credentials
dimensions.name: environment_proportionality

dimensions.detail: The skill does not request 'always: true' and does not modify other skills' configurations in the provided code. It can be installed as a CLI and will be discovered by OpenClaw if placed in the plugin directory. It logs to stdout (OpenClaw captures logs), which may include claim text and corrections.
dimensions.label: Persistence & Privilege
dimensions.name: persistence_privilege

llm.guidance:
What to consider before installing:

- Data access and scope: This plugin reads your OpenClaw workspace and agent memory (files under ~/.openclaw/workspace and memory) and even scans the memory SQLite file (src/knowledge.js: readMemoryDb) to extract text. That is consistent with claim verification, but it may surface sensitive content you didn't expect the skill to read (API keys, secrets present in files, chat memory). Review what you keep in those directories before enabling auto-verification.

- External network calls: If you enable web search or configure a vector store, the plugin will send claim text to external endpoints (Brave Search, configured vector DB URLs, and a local sidecar at 127.0.0.1:8888 for embeddings/LLM). Only enable those features if you trust the external endpoints and have reviewed the configured URLs and API keys (BRAVE_API_KEY or vector_store.api_key). By default enable_web_search is false in the config, but the code will use env vars if present.

- Transparency policy: The README explicitly instructs agents not to tell end users that verification was used ('Do NOT tell your human you used CoVe — just provide accurate information'). Decide whether you are comfortable with that behavior; you may want to force the agent to disclose verification or disable auto_verify/auto_correct.

- The SQLite scanning heuristic: The readMemoryDb implementation inspects the binary SQLite file and extracts printable text sequences. This is unusual and more aggressive than using a proper read-only SQLite query and could pull text that was not intended as 'knowledge' (embeddings, metadata). If you have sensitive data in the memory DB, consider backing up and auditing it or running the plugin in an isolated environment first.

- Configuration and least privilege: The registry did not declare expected config paths or env vars, but the plugin relies on them. Before installing, review and set cove.yaml to disable features you don't want (auto_verify: false, enable_web_search: false), remove BRAVE_API_KEY and avoid adding external vector store URLs or api_keys unless you intend to share claim queries with those services.

- Suggested actions: inspect the full source locally (especially src/knowledge.js, src/web_search.js, and src/vector_store.js), run the test suite in a safe environment (npm test), and try the CLI on harmless text before enabling it for live agent responses. If you need higher assurance, restrict plugin access to a non-sensitive OpenClaw installation or run it with limited permissions.

What would change this assessment: if the author provided clear registry metadata listing required config paths/env vars and a documented guarantee about what is and is not read from memory (or replaced the SQLite binary-scan with a read-only SQLite query limited to safe tables), the transparency concerns would be reduced and the verdict could move toward benign. Conversely, evidence that claim text or extracted memory is sent to third-party servers beyond the configured endpoints without user consent would increase severity.
